outcome: Since 26 January 2024 nothing I could find settles whether B(2,5) is finite or moves the known finite and infinite cases of the classification of B(m,n). The in-window items are: a 2024 journal paper estimating infinitude of initial approximations for odd n > 120 (not of B(m,n) itself); a 2026 survey that mentions the Burnside problem without a new result; a 2026 cost-one result for B(m,n) with odd n >= 665, which uses infinitude rather than establishing it; and an unsourced 2026 AI-lab claim about smaller instances. The odd-exponent threshold of 557 (Atkarskaya, Rips, Tent) was first written down in April 2023, before the window; its March 2024 re-postings carry the same mathematics.
problem_asks: (a) For which positive integers m and n is the free Burnside group B(m,n) finite: classify all pairs (m,n) into finite and infinite. The bullet does not state the trivial cases separately (m = 1 gives a cyclic group; n = 1 gives the trivial group), but the classification covers them. Fixing n and letting m vary, the classification for that n is the Burnside problem for exponent n. (b) In particular, decide whether B(2,5), the free Burnside group on two generators of exponent 5, is finite. The bullet names no field or characteristic and concerns the free group B(m,n), not the restricted Burnside group R(m,n) (the largest finite group of exponent n on m generators), which is a different object.

events.what_happened: Burnside showed that B(m,2) is finite for every m: it is the direct product of m copies of the cyclic group of order 2. This is the first finite case of the classification. Recorded from the Wikipedia article's exponent summary; the 1902 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Finiteness of B(m,2) for every m; settles n = 2 completely.
events.remains: Every exponent n other than 2, including n = 5.
events.directly_checkable: B(m,2) is elementary abelian of order 2^m; the identity x^2 = 1 forces commutativity, so this can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Finite (positive answer for n = 2).

events.what_happened: Sanov showed that B(m,4) is finite for every m. Recorded from the Wikipedia article, which cites Sanov (1940) for exponent 4. The 1940 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Finiteness of B(m,4) for every m; settles n = 4 completely.
events.remains: Every exponent n other than 4, including n = 5.
events.direction: Finite (positive answer for n = 4).

events.what_happened: Marshall Hall, 'Solution of the Burnside problem for exponent six', Illinois J. Math. 2 (1958), 764-786 (received 13 November 1958): B(m,6) is finite for every m, with an explicit order formula. Found through a search snippet of the Project Euclid record and secondary summaries; the article itself was not opened. Some secondary sources date the result 1957; the publication is 1958.
events.delivers: Finiteness of B(m,6) for every m; settles n = 6 completely.
events.remains: Every exponent n other than 6, including n = 5.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; accepted and published the paper in 1958.

events.direction: Finite (positive answer for n = 6).

events.what_happened: A. I. Kostrikin, 'Solution of a weakened problem of Burnside for exponent 5', Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat. 19:3 (1955), 233-244. Recorded as the earliest exponent-5 result. The title says it treats a weakened problem, not B(m,5). Known only from a bibliographic search snippet; not opened.
events.delivers: Per the title only: a weakened form of the Burnside problem for exponent 5. Does not decide the finiteness of the free group B(m,5); discounted for that reason.
events.remains: The finiteness of B(m,5) and of B(2,5) as the bullet asks.
events.doubts: Content not read; the reading that it is a weakened problem rests on the title alone.
events.direction: Unclear from the title; not stated as a finiteness result for B(m,5).

events.what_happened: A. I. Kostrikin, 'On Burnside's problem', Doklady AN SSSR 119:6 (1958), 1081-1084. Per search snippets, it shows that among finite groups with m generators and prime exponent there is a largest one, which solves the restricted Burnside problem for prime exponent (including exponent 5). Not opened; secondary summaries only.
events.delivers: Finiteness of the restricted group R(m,p) for prime p (the largest finite group of exponent p on m generators). This is a different object from B(m,p); by the snippets it does not claim finiteness of B(m,p). Discounted as a restricted analogue.
events.remains: Finiteness of the free group B(m,5) and of B(2,5).
events.doubts: The distinction between restricted and free groups is taken from secondary summaries (Wikipedia: 'Kostrikin ... proved finiteness of B0(m,p)'). The original was not read.
events.direction: Finite, for the restricted group only.

events.what_happened: J. Havas, R. G. Wall and J. B. Wamsley compute the largest finite two-generator group of exponent 5, the restricted Burnside group R(2,5): order 5^34 and class 12, obtained by two independent methods, with a consistent commutator-power presentation. Havas's abstract (search snippet) describes the work as partial evidence for finiteness of the free group B(2,5). Bull. Austral. Math. Soc., 1974. Not opened.
events.delivers: The restricted group R(2,5) has order 5^34. This is the free group B(2,5) only if B(2,5) is finite, which the paper does not establish (partial evidence only, per the abstract summary). Discounted as an analogue (restricted group, not the free group).
events.remains: Whether B(2,5) = R(2,5), i.e. whether B(2,5) is finite; and B(m,5) in general.

checked_by.who: Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society (editorial refereeing)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; accepted and published the paper in 1974.
checked_by.what_they_did: Refereed and published the article; the order was obtained by two independent computations (per the abstract).

events.directly_checkable: The consistent commutator-power presentation given in the paper can be checked for consistency with group-computation software; not checked here.
events.doubts: The source describes partial evidence for finiteness of B(2,5). Several later computational papers (Kuznetsov and coauthors, search summaries) call 5^34 the order of 'the largest two-generator Burnside group of exponent 5'; that phrasing refers to the restricted group, not the free group.
events.direction: Consistent with finiteness of B(2,5) (partial evidence); not a proof that B(2,5) is finite.
events.object: The restricted two-generator group of exponent 5, given by a consistent power-commutator presentation on 34 generators with order 5^34 and class 12; it is a finite group, not a proof about the free group.

events.what_happened: A chapter in Groups - St Andrews 1981 (London Math. Soc. Lecture Note Series) attempts to prove the finiteness of B(5,2) = B(2,5). It shows B(5,2) has a normal subgroup K1 of index 5^10, the normal closure of 24 explicit elements, and reduces finiteness to showing that K1 is abelian (in which case |K1| = 5^24 and the total would be 5^34). Search snippet of the Cambridge listing; OCR renders the exponents as '510' and '524'. The author attribution could not be confirmed; one search summary names Hall and Sims, unverified. Not opened.
events.delivers: A reduction only: if the normal subgroup K1 of index 5^10 is abelian, B(2,5) is finite. The snippet gives no proof that K1 is abelian. Discounted as a conditional reduction, not a resolution.
events.remains: Finiteness of B(2,5), which depends on the unproved abelianness step.
events.doubts: The snippet does not say whether the abelianness of K1 was later established. The order 5^34 of the restricted group is consistent with K1 being abelian of order 5^24, but consistency is not proof. Full text not read.
events.direction: Toward finiteness, conditional on an unproved claim.

events.what_happened: M. Vaughan-Lee's 1990 work on the three-generator case: the largest finite 3-generator group of exponent 5 (the restricted group R(3,5)) has associated Lie ring of dimension 2282, hence order 5^2282 and class 17. Per a search summary of his publication page; not opened.
events.delivers: The restricted three-generator group R(3,5) has order 5^2282. Restricted and three-generator, so discounted as an analogue of B(2,5).
events.remains: B(2,5) and B(3,5) finiteness.
events.doubts: Taken from a search summary of the author's publication list; the paper was not opened.
events.direction: Finite, for the restricted group R(3,5) only.

events.what_happened: P. S. Novikov and S. I. Adian show that B(m,n) is infinite for every m >= 2 and every odd n > 4381 (combinatorial proof). The first negative answer for odd exponents. Recorded from the Wikipedia article; the 1968 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: B(m,n) infinite for every m >= 2 and every odd n > 4381 (threshold as quoted in Wikipedia).
events.remains: Odd n up to 4381; later reduced by Adian to 665 and by others further (see later events).

checked_by.qualification: Research mathematician who wrote the geometric approach to the infinitude of B(m,n) for odd n.
checked_by.what_they_did: Gave an independent geometric proof of the same odd-exponent infinitude (for n > 10^10), 1982.

events.direction: Infinite (negative answer for large odd n).

events.what_happened: S. I. Adian lowers the odd-exponent threshold of the Novikov-Adian theorem to odd n >= 665, in his monograph (cited as 1979 in the Wikipedia article). Not opened; the threshold is also quoted by Atkarskaya, Rips and Tent as the previous best bound.
events.delivers: B(m,n) infinite for every m >= 2 and every odd n >= 665.
events.remains: Odd n below 665 (later reduced to 557 by the 2023 preprint; see that event).
events.doubts: Monograph not read; the threshold is taken from Wikipedia and from the 2023 preprint's introduction.
events.direction: Infinite (negative answer for odd n >= 665).

events.what_happened: A. Yu. Ol'shanskii gives a geometric proof that B(m,n) is infinite for odd n > 10^10 (Wikipedia: 1982, book 1989, translated 1991). Recorded from the Wikipedia summary; not opened.
events.delivers: B(m,n) infinite for m >= 2 and odd n > 10^10, by a geometric method.
events.remains: Odd n between 665 and 10^10 (covered by the combinatorial results), and even n not covered elsewhere.
events.direction: Infinite (negative answer for very large odd n).

events.what_happened: S. V. Ivanov's construction of infinite free Burnside groups for large even exponents: announced in 1992, published 1994 in the International Journal of Algebra and Computation (about 300 pages, per a search summary). The stated threshold differs between sources: Wikipedia gives, for m > 1, even n >= 248 with a divisibility condition; the Encyclopedia of Mathematics (search summary) gives n >= 2^48 with 2^9 dividing n. Neither original was opened.
events.delivers: B(m,n) infinite for m > 1 and for even n in a set described as n >= 2^48 with 2^9 | n (EoM summary) or as n >= 248 with a divisibility condition (Wikipedia summary). The sources disagree on the set.
events.remains: Even exponents outside that set, including all small even n such as 8, 10 and 12; and every odd n as far as this event is concerned.
events.doubts: The threshold conflict above; the original paper was not opened.
events.direction: Infinite (negative answer for large even n).

events.what_happened: I. G. Lysenok, 'Infinite Burnside groups of even exponent', Izvestiya Math. (1996): a negative solution of the Burnside problem for even n >= 8000 (a search snippet quotes the abstract with the sentence on n = 16k >= 8000). Wikipedia summarises this as extending Ivanov's result to m > 1, n >= 8000. Not opened.
events.delivers: B(m,n) infinite for m > 1 and even n >= 8000 (the snippet's second sentence concerns n = 16k).
events.remains: Even n below 8000 that are not covered by the Ivanov construction; all odd n that are not covered by the odd-exponent results.
events.doubts: The snippet quote is partial; the original was not read.
events.direction: Infinite (negative answer for even n >= 8000).

events.what_happened: R. Coulon, 'Infinite periodic groups of even exponents' (arXiv 1810.08372): a new proof that free Burnside groups of sufficiently large even exponents are infinite, using a method for (partially) periodic quotients of groups acting on hyperbolic spaces with a weak acylindricity condition. The abstract gives no numerical threshold and claims no new bound.
events.revisions: v2 6 Nov 2018; v3 3 Dec 2018; v4 14 Jan 2021 (current). No revision in 2024 or 2025 found on the arXiv history page. A search snippet's 'December 2024' date is not supported by that page.
events.delivers: B(m,n) infinite for sufficiently large even n, by a new method. No threshold stated in the abstract, so no movement of the known even-exponent threshold is claimed.
events.remains: Small even n, and every odd n as far as this event is concerned.
events.doubts: Only the abstract was read. No third-party check found.
events.direction: Infinite (negative answer for large even n).

events.what_happened: S. Bachmuth, 'Solvable matrix groups and the Burnside problem' (arXiv math/0609415, 14 Sep 2006). For each prime power q it constructs a solvable matrix group over a quotient of a Laurent polynomial ring, closely related to a group of exponent q, and claims that Burnside groups of exponent q are therefore solvable, with solvability class tending to infinity as q grows. All groups are described as 2-generator. The abstract states no finiteness conclusion.
events.revisions: Single listed version, 14 Sep 2006. Listing comment: Section 5 completely rewritten.
events.delivers: Claimed solvability of 2-generator Burnside groups of prime-power exponent, which would include exponent 5. The abstract does not say whether the groups are free or restricted, and does not state finiteness. If they are free, the claim would bear directly on B(2,5); if restricted, it would concern R(2,5).
events.remains: Everything, unless the claim is accepted and the groups are identified as free Burnside groups.
events.doubts: If the groups are the free groups B(2,q), the claim conflicts with the published odd-exponent infinitude theorems: they give B(2,n) infinite for odd n >= 665, and 3^7 = 2187 is an odd prime power above that threshold. The abstract does not say free or restricted, so the conflict is conditional. No verification or refutation found; the same author's later papers cite this one.
events.direction: Claims solvability (and finiteness is the consequence the author draws in later papers) for 2-generator prime-power exponent groups.

events.what_happened: S. Bachmuth, 'Solution to the Burnside Problem' (arXiv 0803.1612, 11 Mar 2008, 14 pages). Claims a solution for 2-generator groups of prime-power exponent via a 'Generalized Burnside Theorem': a solvability theorem for a family of groups called GB groups, which the abstract says contains infinite as well as finite groups. Most results are said to appear in arXiv:math/0609415 and arXiv:0709.1688.
events.delivers: As claimed: finiteness for 2-generator groups of prime-power exponent, which would include exponent 5. The abstract's main theorem is a solvability theorem for GB groups that include infinite groups, so the finiteness step is not explicit in the abstract. The abstract also says results of Hall and Higman extend finiteness to composite exponents.
events.remains: Unless accepted: B(2,5) and every other 2-generator prime-power exponent case.
events.doubts: Same conditional conflict with the odd-exponent infinitude theorems as the 2006 entry (for free groups at prime-power odd exponents such as 3^7). The abstract's own description of GB groups as containing infinite groups leaves open what finiteness the claim asserts. No published verification or refutation found.
events.direction: Claims finiteness for 2-generator prime-power exponent groups, via solvability.

events.what_happened: S. Bachmuth, 'A straightforward solution to the Burnside Problem' (arXiv 1603.08421, 28 Mar 2016, 22 pages). Abstract: 'We present a solution to the Burnside Problem for 2 generator groups of prime-power exponent.' The approach constructs a surjection from a rank-2 free group onto a solvable group G and shows the Burnside group is an image of G, using a theorem from a paper with Heilbronn and Mochizuki. Listing comment: substantial text overlap with arXiv:0803.1612.
events.delivers: Claimed finiteness of 2-generator Burnside groups of prime-power exponent. Exponent 5 is a prime power, so the claim as worded covers B(2,5) if the groups are the free ones; the abstract does not state B(2,5) finite explicitly and does not say free or restricted.
events.remains: Unless accepted: every 2-generator prime-power exponent case, including B(2,5).
events.doubts: Same conditional conflict with odd prime-power exponents such as 3^7 if the groups are free. The abstract presents the result as a solution; no verification or refutation by another author found in my searches.
events.direction: Claims finiteness for 2-generator prime-power exponent groups.

events.what_happened: A. Atkarskaya, E. Rips and K. Tent, 'The Burnside Problem for Odd Exponents' (arXiv 2303.15997), version 1: free Burnside groups B(m,n) are infinite for m >= 2 and odd n >= 593, described as lowering the previous best odd bound 665 to 593. Superseded by version 2, which states 557. Recorded separately because it is a different claimed threshold.
events.revisions: Superseded: v2 23 Apr 2023 (557); v3 22 Jun 2023; v4 27 Mar 2024; v5 28 Mar 2024.
events.delivers: B(m,n) infinite for m >= 2 and odd n >= 593 (superseded by the 557 version).
events.remains: Odd n below 593, including n = 5.
events.doubts: Superseded within the same preprint; the threshold moved between versions.
events.direction: Infinite (negative answer for odd n >= 593).

events.what_happened: Same preprint, version 2 (23 Apr 2023): free Burnside groups B(m,n) are infinite for m >= 2 and every odd n >= 557 (Theorem 2.1). The abstract says this decreases the best known odd-exponent lower bound from 665 (Adian) to 557. The proof uses iterated small cancellation with an induction on the nesting depth of relators and a new notion of 'certification sequence' (per the abstract as summarised). Version 2 was read through its HTML rendering; the PDF of v2 could not be read with the tools available.
events.revisions: v1 28 Mar 2023 (593, see separate event); v3 22 Jun 2023 (557 unchanged in HTML rendering); v4 27 Mar 2024 (same 557 statement, within the window); v5 28 Mar 2024 (listing comment: 'Small editorial changes, 58pp. Same version with correct arxiv abstract'). By section 5.1 the date is that of the version first carrying the 557 mathematics, v2.
events.delivers: Infinitude of B(m,n) for every m >= 2 and every odd n >= 557. This answers the classification in the negative for odd n >= 557 and only for odd n.
events.remains: (a) Odd n with 5 <= n <= 555, including n = 5, the case of B(2,5) itself; and every even n, which this paper does not treat. (b) The finiteness of B(2,5) is untouched.
events.doubts: (i) No journal publication found in my searches. (ii) The threshold moved from 593 to 557 between v1 and v2, and the introduction states the argument 'currently needs n > 36·15+16 = 556'. (iii) A search summary (unverified; relayed from a summary of Lysenok's 2023 paper) says Lysenok notes several announced lower-bound results exist but that the lowest carefully checked bound he cites is the older one. (iv) The 2026 Donoso-Echenique and Silva abstract states the odd threshold as 665, not 557. None of these is a specific error in the argument; I found none.
events.direction: Infinite: B(m,n) infinite for all odd n >= 557 and all m >= 2.

events.what_happened: I. G. Lysenok, 'A sample iterated small cancellation theory for groups of Burnside type' (arXiv 2301.05000, 12 Jan 2023). Presents B(m,n), m >= 2, odd n, as satisfying an iterated small-cancellation condition and gives 'a reasonably accessible proof that B(m,n) is infinite' for odd n > 2000. Published in Izvestiya: Mathematics 89:4 (2025), pp. 758-861 (received 10 March 2023; published 25 August 2025 on the English record, 15 August 2025 on the Russian record, per mathnet.ru).
events.revisions: Single arXiv version (v1, 12 Jan 2023; 97 pages). Journal version: Izv. Math. 89:4 (2025), DOI 10.4213/im9475e (per mathnet). The 2025 publication is a journal event, not the first public argument.
events.delivers: B(m,n) infinite for m >= 2 and odd n > 2000. This threshold is weaker than Adian's 665 and the 2023 preprint's 557, so it moves no known threshold.
events.remains: Odd n <= 2000, including n = 5 (B(2,5) itself), and every even n not covered elsewhere.

checked_by.who: Izvestiya: Mathematics (editorial refereeing; Steklov Institute / Russian Academy of Sciences journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; accepted the paper for publication in 2025 after receipt on 10 March 2023.

events.doubts: Only the abstract and introduction summary were read. The journal refereeing is the only public check found.
events.direction: Infinite (negative answer for odd n > 2000).

events.what_happened: A. Beletskiy and I. Ivanov-Pogodaev, 'Combinatorial Estimations on Burnside Type Problems', Mathematics (MDPI) 12(5), article 665 (issue dated February 2024). The abstract says it gives a self-contained exposition of E. Rips's iterative small cancellation theory and uses it 'to obtain new estimates on the infiniteness of initial approximations of Burnside groups where only a finite number of periodic relations is used for relatively small odd exponents (n > 120)'. A search summary says the paper cites the 2023 Atkarskaya-Rips-Tent preprint and describes the work as joint with Rips and Tent. The publisher page was blocked to every route I tried; the abstract was read from the IDEAS/RePEc record.
events.delivers: Estimates of infinitude of initial approximations (groups given by finitely many periodic relations) for odd n > 120. Per the abstract this concerns approximations, not B(m,n) itself. The abstract does not say whether it yields infinitude of B(m,n) for any odd n in 121 to 556.
events.remains: Whether B(m,n) is infinite for odd n between 121 and 556 (not stated in the abstract); all of the even-exponent gap; B(2,5).

checked_by.who: MDPI, journal Mathematics (peer-reviewed); referees not named
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the article.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published after review according to the journal's policy; the referee reports were not seen.

events.doubts: Full text not read: the publisher site returned HTTP 403 for every route (page, /htm, /pdf, DOI redirect). The reading that it does not bear on B(m,n) rests on the abstract alone. The day of publication comes from a search summary of the publisher page, not from a page I could open. Competing reading: if the estimates imply infinitude of B(m,n) for odd n > 120, the odd threshold would move from 557 to 121; the abstract does not say so.
events.direction: No direction for B(m,n) stated; it concerns infinite initial approximations, an intermediate object.
events.object: Not stated in the abstract. The objects are initial approximations of Burnside groups, built from finitely many periodic relations, which the paper shows are infinite for odd n > 120. Whether these are explicit is not stated in the abstract.

events.what_happened: The Laboratory for AI in Algebra at Bar-Ilan University (director Elena Bunina; Kyrylo Muliarchyk listed as postdoc) states on its web page that its reinforcement-learning 'RL Algorithmic Mixer' (several specialised algorithms with an ML orchestrator) 'outperforms currently available single-algorithm methods on smaller instances of the Burnside problem'. The page gives no instances, numbers, comparison metric, paper or preprint. The page's last-update stamp is 09/02/2026.
events.revisions: The date is the page's 'last updated' stamp, not its first posting; the first posting date is unknown.
events.delivers: Nothing established about the finiteness of any B(m,n). It is an unquantified computational claim about unspecified smaller instances of the Burnside problem.
events.remains: All of the problem.
events.doubts: The claim is unsupported on the page: no instances, data, method description, or citation. Kyrylo Muliarchyk is also named in an unverified LinkedIn post about a 'Maidenhead Project' with claimed Kourovka solutions; that search did not connect the two projects beyond the shared name.
events.direction: None stated.

events.what_happened: K. Tent, 'From the Cherlin-Zilber Conjecture via sharply 2-transitive groups to the Burnside problem' (arXiv 2606.18207, 16 Jun 2026). A review of the Cherlin-Zilber algebraicity conjecture on simple groups of finite Morley rank. It says sharply 2-transitive groups are a potential source of counterexamples 'and how the Burnside problem necessarily comes into the picture'. The abstract claims no new theorem about B(m,n).
events.delivers: Nothing about the finiteness of any B(m,n): a survey placing the Burnside problem within a model-theoretic search for counterexamples.
events.remains: All of the problem.
events.doubts: Abstract only; the full text was not read.
events.direction: None stated for B(m,n).

events.what_happened: M. Donoso-Echenique and E. Silva, 'Free Burnside groups of large odd exponent have cost 1' (arXiv 2608.20472, v1 20 Aug 2026, v2 21 Sep 2026). For a non-elementary torsion-free hyperbolic group H and large odd n, H/H^n has cost 1; for H free of rank m >= 2 they state that B(m,n) has cost 1 for every odd n >= 665, hence is anti-treeable with vanishing first l^2-Betti number. This recovers Feldkamp and Kionke (2023) for large prime exponents.
events.delivers: Cost one and vanishing first l^2-Betti number for B(m,n), odd n >= 665, m >= 2. These are properties of groups already known to be infinite; the paper does not address finiteness of any B(m,n).
events.remains: The finiteness question for every (m,n), including B(2,5).
events.doubts: Abstract only. Its odd threshold is 665, the older bound, not the 557 of the 2023 preprint; the abstract does not cite the 557 result.
events.direction: Uses the infinite side (B(m,n) infinite for odd n >= 665) rather than establishing it.

disputes.summary: Several sources give 5^34 as the order of 'the largest two-generator Burnside group of exponent 5' (Krause and Weston, Havas-Wall-Wamsley, Kuznetsov and coauthors), and some search summaries state that B(2,5) is finite. That group is the restricted group R(2,5). The current Wikipedia Burnside article states that 'the particular case of B(2,5) remains open'. I record Wikipedia's reading as the status of the question, and the restricted-group reading as what the 5^34 sources establish.

Bachmuth's arXiv papers (math/0609415 in 2006, 0803.1612 in 2008, 1603.08421 in 2016) claim solvability or finiteness of 2-generator Burnside groups of prime-power exponent. I found no acceptance, no refutation and no retraction in the literature searched. If the groups are free, the claims conflict with the published odd-exponent infinitude results at prime-power exponents such as 3^7 = 2187. The abstracts do not say whether the groups are free or restricted.

Ivanov's even-exponent threshold is stated differently in sources: Wikipedia gives even n >= 248 with a divisibility condition (rendered 'divisible by 29' in the summary), while the Encyclopedia of Mathematics (search summary) gives n >= 2^48 with 2^9 | n. Lysenok's 1996 paper gives even n >= 8000. Not resolved; neither original was opened.

summary: The problem asks for the classification of pairs (m,n) with B(m,n) finite, and in particular whether B(2,5) is finite. The sources I could open establish the following. Finiteness is known for n = 2, 3, 4, 6 and all m (Burnside; Sanov 1940; M. Hall 1958; the n = 3 case is credited to Burnside in Wikipedia, year not checked and not recorded as an event). Infinitude is known for odd n >= 4381 (Novikov-Adian 1968), n >= 665 (Adian), n > 10^10 (Ol'shanskii 1982), and now for odd n >= 557 (Atkarskaya-Rips-Tent, preprint, first version with 557 dated 23 April 2023), and for even n >= 8000 (Lysenok 1996, with Ivanov 1994 covering large even n under thresholds the sources disagree on). Lysenok's 2023 preprint (journal 2025) gives odd n > 2000. Wikipedia's current article states that B(2,5) remains open. The 5^34 results (Kostrikin's bound, Havas-Wall-Wamsley 1974) concern the restricted group R(2,5), and the 1981 St Andrews reduction is conditional on an unproved abelianness claim. Bachmuth's arXiv claims of finiteness for 2-generator prime-power exponent groups (2006, 2008, 2016) are unaccepted and, for free groups, conflict with the odd-exponent theorems. Within the window (from 26 January 2024), the events are: (i) the March 2024 v4 and v5 re-postings of the 557 preprint, which carry the 2023 mathematics and make only editorial changes; (ii) the MDPI paper of February 2024, whose abstract estimates infinitude of initial approximations for odd n > 120, not of B(m,n) itself; (iii) Tent's June 2026 ICM survey, which mentions the Burnside problem but claims no new theorem; (iv) Donoso-Echenique and Silva's August 2026 cost-one result for B(m,n) with odd n >= 665, which uses infinitude and does not establish any finiteness; (v) the Bar-Ilan AI lab's undated-first-posting web claim (last updated 9 February 2026) that its RL-based method beats single-algorithm methods on 'smaller instances of the Burnside problem', with no instances, numbers, or paper. Judged on the sources I could open, nothing in the window changes the status of B(2,5), which remains open. The AI search found no AI system credited with any Burnside result in any source. The 2026 Kourovka papers (arXiv 2607.17477, Aristotle/Harmonic; arXiv 2608.29219, credited to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 as read through an HTML summary) address other problems, per their abstracts and summaries. The OpenAI 'Astra' announcement of August 2026 (non-sofic group, via news coverage) and the Maidenhead Project LinkedIn claims (24 Kourovka solutions, unverified) do not touch the Burnside problem in what I could see. Close calls: (a) the 557 bound is first public in April 2023, so it is pre-window even though its re-postings are in 2024; (b) the MDPI paper could be read as moving the odd threshold to 121 if its approximation estimates implied infinitude of B(m,n), but its abstract does not say that and I could not open the text; (c) the Bar-Ilan claim is AI-involved in a computational sense, but names no system and gives no result.
competing_reading: Read the window more generously: the MDPI paper (Feb 2024) is the only peer-reviewed in-window item that bears on the odd-exponent classification, and if its estimates for odd n > 120 are in fact estimates of infinitude of B(m,n) rather than of initial approximations, the odd threshold would have moved from 557 to 121 within the window. The abstract, read from the IDEAS record, says initial approximations, and the full text was blocked. A second reading treats the March 2024 re-postings (v4, v5) as the publication of the 557 result, dating it into the window; the arXiv history shows the 557 statement already in v2 (April 2023), so I date it there. A third reading takes the 5^34 literature as settling B(2,5): that reading equates the restricted group R(2,5) with the free group B(2,5), and Wikipedia's current text rejects it.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Beletskiy and Ivanov-Pogodaev (Mathematics 12(5), 665, 2024): whether its main theorem asserts infinitude of B(m,n) for odd n > 120 or only of initial approximations. (2) The PDF of arXiv 2303.15997 v2 (April 2023), to confirm that the 557 statement is first made there and not in a later version. (3) A journal reference for 2303.15997, if one exists. (4) The original 1974 Havas-Wall-Wamsley and 1981 St Andrews texts, to see whether B(2,5) and R(2,5) are distinguished and whether K1 is shown abelian. (5) Any published proof or refutation of the finiteness of B(2,5); a Lean or GAP certificate would count as machine evidence but not as a human reading. (6) Bachmuth's papers' scope (free or restricted groups) and any referee or journal report on them. (7) The body of the Bar-Ilan claim: which instances, what comparison, and whether it is published.

incomplete: (1) The MDPI paper (Beletskiy and Ivanov-Pogodaev, Mathematics 2024) was not read beyond the IDEAS abstract: the publisher site returned HTTP 403 on every route, so its main theorem, the exact scope of the 'infinite initial approximations' statement, its references, its acknowledgements and its AI statement are all unchecked; its publication day (24 February 2024) comes from a search summary of the publisher page. (2) The PDFs of arXiv 2303.15997 v1 and v2 could not be read (binary output). The 593 (v1) and 557 (v2) readings come from the abs page and HTML renderings processed by a summariser; the v2 reading in particular rests on the HTML rendering and should be confirmed from the PDF. The v3, v4 and v5 texts were read only through summaries, and the acknowledgements and contribution statements were not inspected for AI use. (3) Pre-window events were recorded from secondary sources (Wikipedia, search snippets, Cambridge/AMS/Mathnet/Project Euclid listings) and not from the originals: Burnside 1902, Sanov 1940, Hall 1958, Kostrikin 1955 and 1958, Havas-Wall-Wamsley 1974, the St Andrews 1981 chapter, Vaughan-Lee 1990, Novikov-Adian 1968, Adian 1979, Ol'shanskii 1982, Ivanov 1994, Lysenok 1996. The n = 3 finiteness case is not recorded as an event because I did not establish its date. (4) Lysenok 2023/2025 and Coulon 2018 were read through abstracts, not full texts. (5) The 2026 Kourovka papers (2607.17477, 2608.29219) were read through abstracts and an HTML summary, not full texts; neither is claimed to touch the Burnside problem by any source I read, but full texts were not checked for it. (6) The Bar-Ilan claim has no first-posting date; its only date is the page's last-update stamp. No paper behind it was found. (7) No access to MathSciNet, zbMATH, Google Scholar, or the Kourovka Notebook's own 21st-issue text; the body of the 21st issue was not checked for any Burnside-related solution. (8) The LinkedIn claims about the Maidenhead Project and the OpenAI 'Astra' coverage are secondary and unverified. (9) The author of the 1981 St Andrews chapter could not be confirmed. (10) Judgement on whether any event moves the classification, and on whether the 2026 Donoso-Echenique and Silva result or the 2024 MDPI estimates count, is left to the later pass.
